Contextual Non-Convex Bandit Optimization
with Two-Point Feedback

Khaled Eldowa Email: khaled.eldowa@inria.fr Affiliation:     Pierre Gaillard Email: pierre.gaillard@inria.fr Affiliation: 
Abstract

We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

keywords
Contextual Bandits, Online Non-Convex Optimization, Non-Parametric Policies.

1 Introduction

Many modern bandit problems are contextual and non-convex: at every round a decision maker observes side information (a context), must commit to an action in a possibly large and structured action set 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, and only observes the losses of played actions. Examples include dynamic pricing, bidding and ad placement, adaptive control and hyperparameter tuning, where the quality of an action is only observable through a noisy or adversarial evaluation. A natural benchmark in these settings is a rich, nonparametric class of policies 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} mapping contexts to actions, for example all Lipschitz or Hölder-smooth functions. The price of considering such large nonparametric classes is a potentially slower sublinear regret rate, with the rate determined by the complexity of both the action space and the policy class, as quantified by their covering numbers and metric entropy, respectively. The achievable regret rate depends strongly on the feedback model (see related work below). In this work, we are considering a setting, detailed below, that reveals more information about the loss function than standard bandit feedback.

Setting.

Suppose we have an action set 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, a context set 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, and a policy set 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} consisting of functions mapping 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Assume moreover that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is equipped with a metric 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} with respect to which it has a finite diameter. Define the loss set ℒ{\mathcal{L}} as the set of 11-Lipschitz functions mapping 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} to ℝ\mathbb{R}.11 1 For our purposes, one can also start with a generic loss set ℒ{\mathcal{L}} and take 𝔡⁡(a,b)≔supℓ∈ℒ|ℓ⁡(a)−ℓ⁡(b)|{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b)\coloneqq\sup_{{\ell}\in{\mathcal{L}}}|{\ell}(a)-{\ell}(b)| assuming the supremum is finite and non-zero for any pair of distinct actions. We consider an oblivious environment that chooses at every round tt a context xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in{\mathcal{X}} and a (possibly nonconvex) loss function ℓt∈ℒ{\ell}_{t}\in{\mathcal{L}}. After observing the context xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in{\mathcal{X}}, the learner selects two actions At,1A_{t,1} and At,2A_{t,2} in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, observes the difference between their losses ℓt​(At,1)−ℓt​(At,2){\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2}), and suffers their average. The goal is to minimize the regret after TT rounds:

RegT,2≔𝔼⁡[∑t=1T12​(ℓt​(At,1)+ℓt​(At,2))]−inf𝒽∈𝒫∑t=1Tℓt​(𝒽⁡(xt)).\bm{\regret}_{T,2}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{2}\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})+{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})\bigr)\right]-\inf_{{\mathcal{h}}\in{\mathcal{P}}}\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}{\ell}_{t}({\mathcal{h}}(x_{t}))\,.

This model captures online decision problems in which a platform serves two users under the same market conditions and where both outcomes count towards performance. In online advertising, for instance, the platform can show two users sharing the same context xtx_{t} (query, time of day, etc.) two different ads (or bids) At,1A_{t,1} and At,2A_{t,2}. The loss function ℓt{\ell}_{t} encodes the latent market conditions (competing bids, demand, seasonality, etc.), which are common to both users and possibly adversarial. Similarly, a navigation app can recommend two alternative routes to two drivers with the same origin–destination pair and departure time, and observe their travel times (or their difference) under the same traffic conditions. In both examples, a reasonable performance measure is the average (or sum) of the losses of the two played actions.

The central question of this work is to quantify the effect of two-point feedback in nonparametric nonconvex online learning: in particular when can the T\sqrt{T} rate of online convex optimization be recovered in this harder nonparametric bandit framework?

Contributions.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    A generic algorithm and regret bound (Section 2). We introduce an algorithm for contextual bandits with two-point feedback that operates over a generic tree of policy classes (𝒢l)l=0L({\mathcal{G}}_{l})_{l=0}^{{{L}}}, see \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts. If the tree hierarchically approximates the policy class 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} (in the sense of Assumption 1 below), then \Crefthm:generic-thm establishes the following regret bound:

    RegT,2≲(∑l2−2l/3(|𝒜l−1→l|⋅ln|𝒢l|)1/3)3/2T+2−LT,\textstyle\smash{\bm{\regret}_{T,2}\lesssim\Big(\sum_{{l}}2^{-2{l}/3}\big(|{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}|\cdot\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{l}|\big)^{1/3}\Big)^{3/2}\sqrt{T}+2^{-{{L}}}T\,,}

    where |𝒢l||{\mathcal{G}}_{l}| is the number of policies at level l{l} of the tree; and |𝒜l−1→l||{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}| is the number of possible pairs of actions (al−1,al)∈𝒜2(a_{{l}-1},a_{{l}})\in{\mathcal{A}}^{2} such that al−1a_{{l}-1} can be refined into ala_{{l}} by a parent-child pair of functions in the policy tree between levels l−1{l}-1 and l{l}. The generality of this result comes at a cost however: the bound takes an abstract form, and the corresponding algorithm is not computationally efficient in general.

  • •

    Concrete rates (Section 3). For action spaces with covering dimension d{{d}} and finite doubling dimension, and policy classes with metric-entropy exponent p{{p}}, we instantiate the construction of the policy tree and prove a regret of order

    Twhend+p<2,T​(ln⁡T)3/2whend+p=2,andT1−1/(d+p)otherwise.\sqrt{T}\quad\text{when}\quad{{d}}+{{p}}<2,\quad\sqrt{T}(\ln T)^{3/2}\quad\text{when}\quad{{d}}+{{p}}=2,\quad\text{and}\quad T^{1-1/({{d}}+{{p}})}\quad\text{otherwise}\,.

    In particular, this is essentially the full-information rate when d+p≤2{{d}}+{{p}}\leq 2, so two-point feedback closes the gap with full information in these regimes, and improves substantially over the best rates known under one-point feedback. Table 1 summarizes the known rates. For instance, if 𝒜⊆ℝ{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, 𝒳⊆ℝm{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{{{m}}}, and the policy set 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} consists of β{\beta}-Hölder smooth functions from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, we have p=m/β{{p}}={{{m}}}/{{\beta}} and d=1{{{d}}}=1, which entails the full-information T\sqrt{T} rate as soon as the smoothness parameter β{\beta} is larger than the context dimension m{{m}}. Note that in the one-point bandit feedback framework, T\sqrt{T} is not achievable, even in the simplest setting when d=1{{d}}=1 with no contexts (i.e., constant policies), where the minimax rate is T2/3T^{2/3} (Kleinberg et al., 2008).

  • •

    A more efficient implementation for Lipschitz policies (Section 4). For the set of Lipschitz policies from 𝒳:=[0,1]m{\mathcal{X}}:=[0,1]^{{m}} to 𝒜:=[0,1]d{\mathcal{A}}:=[0,1]^{{d}}, we provide a more efficient implementation (Algorithm 4.2) that is shown to be essentially equivalent to the generic Algorithm 2.2. This is done by designing a policy tree with a separable structure, which allows merging known information on the past performance of different policies in a more compact format. In particular, for a fixed d{{{d}}}, the overall space complexity of Algorithm 4.2 is 𝒪⁡(T​ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\ln T), while its per-round time complexity is only 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T). When m=d=1{{m}}={{d}}=1, our algorithm recovers the full-information T\sqrt{T} rate up to logarithmic factors but at a much lower computational cost compared to existing full-information procedures that are either non-constructive (Rakhlin et al., 2015) or require polynomial in TT per-round complexities to leverage the full-information feedback (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2017).

Relation to previous work.

Our work builds on two lines of research: nonconvex nonparametric online learning, and multi-point feedback in bandit and zeroth-order optimization. Within the first line, we also discuss the common technique of building a hierarchical covering of the policy set.

  • •

    Nonconvex nonparametric online learning. With full information, i.e., when the entire loss function is revealed, most existing work considers convex losses. The case of generic Lipschitz loss is considered in Hazan and Megiddo (2007); Rakhlin et al. (2015); Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2017) and the rate is well understood. For a policy class with metric entropy of order ε−p\varepsilon^{-p} (see \Crefdef:metric_entropy), the minimax rate is T\sqrt{T} when p≤2p\leq 2 and T(p−1)/pT^{(p-1)/p} when p>2p>2 achieved by a nonconstructive procedure in Rakhlin et al. (2015) and for Lipschitz policies with a polynomial algorithm in Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2017). The lower bound is due to Hazan and Megiddo (2007). With one-point bandit feedback, where only the loss of the played action is revealed, the exponent degrades markedly; for Lipschitz losses and policies, the best known rates (Slivkins, 2011; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2017) are polynomially worse than their full-information counterparts. In particular, when the covering number of the action set scales as ε−d\varepsilon^{-d} (see \Crefdef:covering), the best known rate is 𝒪~​(T(d+p+1)/(d+p+2))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{\nicefrac{{(d+p+1)}}{{(d+p+2)}}}).

    Recovering the full-information exponent under bandit feedback is impossible in general (Kleinberg et al., 2008; Bubeck et al., 2011), and the gap between the two regimes is an obstacle to deploying nonparametric contextual methods in practice. In this work, we therefore consider the intermediate model of two-point bandit feedback that has not been considered in nonparametric online learning. The intermediate feedback model of one-sided feedback was considered by Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2017) but it is a stronger feedback restricted to one-dimensional action sets and narrower applications (such as online auctions); moreover, they only considered Lipschitz classes of policies.

  • •

    Hierarchical tree covering of the policy set. A key technique in nonparametric online learning consists in building a tree that hierarchically approximates the policy set with increasing levels of precision. This was first used in online learning by Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (1999) for linear loss functions, by Rakhlin and Sridharan (2014); Rakhlin and Sridharan (2015) and Rakhlin et al. (2015) to design nonconstructive procedures achieving the minimax rates in several nonparametric online frameworks, by Gaillard and Gerchinovitz (2015) to build a constructive minimax algorithm in online nonparametric regression, and later by Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2017) for nonparametric bandits with one-sided feedback. An analogous technique was also used by Eldowa et al. (2026) for (non-contextual) structured bandits with two-point feedback, where they construct a tree over the actions.

    The key idea is that when the losses are Lipschitz, two nearby actions have a small loss difference, which, if observable, can allow building a loss estimator with small variance. A tree structure where the nodes at successive levels cover the actions at decreasing scales provides a regular and simple representation of the metric (and hence the loss) structure, which can be exploited by adapting standard algorithmic frameworks. The same applies when the decision space is one of policies instead of actions, as the distance between policies can be measured, for example, by the sup metric. In this work, we leverage our access to loss differences and employ this hierarchical discretization idea to our particular setting of contextual bandit optimization with two-point feedback. Importantly, we explore in the process the challenges (and achievable results) brought about when combining said technique with EXP4-style algorithms common in the contextual bandit space (Auer et al., 2002).

    Outside nonparametric problems, abstract bandit models with hierarchical action spaces are not uncommon in the literature. Most relevant here is the work of Martin et al. (2022), who relied on semi-bandit feedback to leverage the structure of a nested action set, and its expert-advice extension in (Zenati, 2023, Section 5.5), where a finite and unstructured comparator class of experts was considered.

  • •

    Two-point bandit feedback. Multi-point bandit feedback has been considered in order to achieve improved performance compared to one-point bandit feedback. In (non-contextual) bandit convex optimization and zeroth-order optimization, a line of works (Agarwal et al., 2010; Duchi et al., 2015; Shamir, 2017; Lu et al., 2024) showed that two-point feedback, by reducing the variance of the gradient estimator, allows retrieving several benefits of the full-information setting, including a straightforward path to achieving the O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) minimax rate. However, those results rely on convexity of the losses, on gradient estimators, and on having a parametric comparator. None of this is available here: our losses are only Lipschitz (no convexity or differentiability assumed), and the comparator set is a nonparametric class of functions. Similar improvements were shown in standard multi-armed bandits (Sani et al., 2014; Thune and Seldin, 2018; Degenne et al., 2018). However, in those works the extra observation is free, whereas here both played actions incur loss, which is more realistic in many applications.

    Closest to this work is Eldowa et al. (2026), which considers a similar two-point feedback framework and shows that it allows leveraging the structure of the action set. In particular, they recover the T\sqrt{T} full-information rate in one or two-dimensional Lipschitz bandits. They however did not incorporate contexts and did not consider non-parametric policy classes. To our knowledge, the effect of two-point feedback in this regime has not been quantified.

2 A Generic Result

In this section, we provide a generic algorithm that works on hierarchical trees that approximate the policy set. We first detail the tree approximation structure and the approximation properties that are required by our analysis and then present our algorithm together with its regret upper bound.

2.1 Hierarchical tree covering of the policy set

Fix a positive integer L{{L}} and let (𝒜l)l=0L({\mathcal{A}}_{l})_{{l}=0}^{{L}} be a sequence of finite subsets of actions in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} such that 𝒜0≔{a∗}{\mathcal{A}}_{0}\coloneqq\{a^{*}\} for some a∗∈𝒜a^{*}\in{\mathcal{A}}. Assume we are given a sequence (ℱl)l=0L({\mathcal{F}}_{l})_{{l}=0}^{{L}} of finite sets of functions mapping 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} such that ℱ0≔{f0}{\mathcal{F}}_{0}\coloneqq\{{f}_{0}\} for some function f0{f}_{0}, and img⁡(f)⊆𝒜l{\mathrm{img}}({f})\subseteq{\mathcal{A}}_{l} for any f∈ℱl{f}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{l}. Both of these sequences are allowed to contain overlapping sets. We now use (ℱl)l=0L({\mathcal{F}}_{l})_{{l}=0}^{{L}} to build a tree of functions. The set of nodes at level l{l} is given by 𝒢l≔{(l,f)}f∈ℱl{\mathcal{G}}_{l}\coloneqq\{({l},{f})\}_{{f}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{l}}; nevertheless, to declutter the notation, we refer to members of 𝒢l{\mathcal{G}}_{l} simply via the functions they represent, and treat it as a set of functions in some statements. In addition, we assume we are provided a parenthood function acting on all the nodes. In particular, the parent of f∈𝒢l{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l} is denoted by 𝔭⁡(f)∈𝒢l−1{\mathfrak{p}}({f})\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{l}-1}. Building on this, an ancestor function can be defined over the nodes in an obvious manner: 𝔞​𝔫l​(f)≔f{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}\coloneqq{f} for f∈𝒢l{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l} and 𝔞​𝔫l​(f)≔𝔭⁡(𝔞​𝔫l+1​(f)){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}\coloneqq{{\mathfrak{p}}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}+1}({f})}) for f∈𝒢l′{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{l}^{\prime}} with l′>l{l}^{\prime}>{l}. We refer to the resulting tree of functions as 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}).

We ask that 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}) should possess two properties. The first is that 𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}, the functions at the last level, approximate well the competitor space 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}, with a precision proportional to 2−L2^{-{{L}}}. This would allow us to use 𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} as a discrete surrogate for 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}. The second property is that proximity in the function tree translates to similarity of behaviour. To make this concrete we define a notion of distance between functions: for f,f′:𝒳→𝒜{f},{f}^{\prime}\colon{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{A}}, define

𝔡∞​(f,f′)≔supx∈𝒳𝔡⁡(f⁡(x),f′​(x)).\textstyle{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({f},{f}^{\prime})\coloneqq\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}{\mathfrak{d}}({f}(x),{f}^{\prime}(x))\,.

This is a metric over 𝒜𝒳{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}}, the set of all functions mapping 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. We can now state precisely the assumption that our algorithm will operate under.

Assumption 1.

There exist two positive constants Capx{C}_{\mathrm{apx}} and Cprt{C}_{\mathrm{prt}} such that

  1. 1.

    𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} is a Capx​2−L{C}_{\mathrm{apx}}2^{-{{L}}}-(external) cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} with respect to 𝔡∞;{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}\,;

  2. 2.

    𝔡∞​(𝔭⁡(f),f)≤Cprt​2−l{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({{\mathfrak{p}}}({f}),{f})\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}} for f∈𝒢l+1.{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{l}+1}\,.

To demonstrate the utility of the second property, observe that any f,f′∈𝒢L{f},{f}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} satisfying 𝔞​𝔫l​(f)=𝔞​𝔫l​(f′){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}^{\prime})} also satisfy via the triangle inequality that

𝔡∞​(f,f′)\displaystyle{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({f},{f}^{\prime}) ≤∑j=l+1L𝔡∞​(𝔞​𝔫j​(f),𝔞​𝔫j−1​(f))+𝔡∞​(𝔞​𝔫j​(f′),𝔞​𝔫j−1​(f′))≤4​Cprt​2−l.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j={l}+1}^{{{L}}}{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{j}({f})},{{\mathfrak{an}}_{j-1}({f})})+{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{j}({f}^{\prime})},{{\mathfrak{an}}_{j-1}({f}^{\prime})})\leq 4{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}}\,.

These sets might overlap for different actions in 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l}. Notice now that the second property in \Crefassump:function-tree is equivalent to asking that for a∈𝒜la\in{\mathcal{A}}_{l} and b∈𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l+1​(a)b\in{\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}+1}(a), 𝔡⁡(a,b)≤Cprt​2−l.{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b)\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}}\,.

2.2 Algorithm and regret upper bound

We are now ready to present \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts. We use Δ𝒢,L{{\Delta}}_{{\mathcal{G}},{{L}}} to denote the space of probability distributions over 𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}; also, ℙ(⋅∣𝔉t−1)\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t-1}) and 𝔼[⋅∣𝔉t−1]\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t-1}] are denoted by ℙt​(⋅)\mathbb{P}_{t}(\cdot) and 𝔼t​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{t}[\cdot] respectively, where 𝔉t{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the random events up to the end of round tt. The algorithm is an instance of the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) template executed on the leaves 𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}. It builds upon Algorithm 1 of Eldowa et al. (2026), and in particular, extends its idea to the contextual (experts) setting via an EXP4-style estimator (Auer et al., 2002). Having observed xtx_{t}, the idea is to extend the cost function 𝐜t​(f):=ℓt​(f⁡(xt)){\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f}):={\ell}_{t}({f}(x_{t})) to the internal nodes of the tree, so that we can write 𝐜t​(f)=∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f)){\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})=\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{\mathbf{c}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}) up to an additive constant, see \Creflem:telescoping-nodeloss in \Crefapp:generic-analysis. The value of 𝐜t,l​(f′){\mathbf{c}}_{t,{l}}({f}^{\prime}) for some f′∈𝒢l{f}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l} is (up to a small constant shift) the expected value of the difference between the losses of two random actions: the first is distributed as f⁡(xt){f}(x_{t}) with f∼pt|𝔞​𝔫l​(f)​(xt)=f′​(xt){f}\sim p_{t}\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t})={f}^{\prime}(x_{t}), and the second as f⁡(xt){f}(x_{t}) with f∼pt|𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)​(xt)=𝔭⁡(f′)​(xt){f}\sim p_{t}\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t})={\mathfrak{p}}({f}^{\prime})(x_{t}). Thanks to the second item in \Crefassump:function-tree, 𝐜t,l​(f′){\mathbf{c}}_{t,{l}}({f}^{\prime}) is 𝒪⁡(2−l)\mathcal{O}(2^{-{l}}). Note that 𝐜t,l​(f′){\mathbf{c}}_{t,{l}}({f}^{\prime}) provides information about all f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} with 𝔞​𝔫l​(f)​(xt)=f′​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t})={f}^{\prime}(x_{t}) and 𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)​(xt)=𝔭⁡(f′)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t})={\mathfrak{p}}({f}^{\prime})(x_{t}); that is, all the leaves f{f} whose ancestors at levels l{l} and l−1{l}-1 behave like, respectively, f′{f}^{\prime} and 𝔭⁡(f′){\mathfrak{p}}({f}^{\prime}) on xtx_{t}.

With two-point feedback, we can compute an estimate of this value for one (randomly selected) node of the tree by sampling a pair of actions in the manner we just described. The node selected in \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts is 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}, and the two sampled actions are At,1=ft,1​(xt)A_{t,1}={f}_{t,1}(x_{t}) and At,2=ft,2​(xt)A_{t,2}={f}_{t,2}(x_{t}), whose distributions are consistent with our discussion above applied to the value of 𝐜t,lt​(𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt)){\mathbf{c}}_{t,{l}_{t}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}). This is then used to build an importance-weighted loss estimate 𝐜^t​(f)\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f}) for all leaves f{f}, which is active only if 𝔞​𝔫lt​(f){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({f})} and 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(f){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({f})} output the same actions as 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})} and 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})} at xtx_{t}. This provides a generic regret bound for any hierarchical tree satisfying Assumption 1. The bound scales with level-wise quantities |𝒜l−1→l||{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}| and |𝒢l||{\mathcal{G}}_{l}| that will be made explicit in the next section to provide concrete rates. For now, observe that a naive application of the non-contextual algorithm of Eldowa et al. (2026) would yield via their Corollary 4 a similar-looking bound with (|𝒜l−1→l|​ln⁡|𝒢l|)1/3\left(|{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}|\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{l}|\right)^{1/3} replaced by |𝒢l|1/3|{\mathcal{G}}_{l}|^{1/3}. This improvement is thanks to \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts exploiting the problem structure; particularly, that information can be shared between policies such that in the end, what matters is the number of possible action pairs |𝒜l−1→l||{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}| instead of the number of policies.

A reminiscent result was obtained by Zenati (2023) who considered an experts problem over a nested action set (extending the nested bandits setting of Martin et al. 2022), and used an EXP4-type algorithm. Their setting requires a stronger semi-bandit feedback, in which the learner observes L{{L}} intermediate losses induced by a given hierarchical decomposition of the played action. Nonetheless, in our notation, their regret upper bound (Theorem 5.5.1) would look like

∑l=1L2−l|𝒜l−1→l|​T​ln⁡|𝒢L|≥1L(∑l=1L2−2l/3(|𝒜l−1→l|ln|𝒢L|)1/3)3/2T.\textstyle\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}2^{-{l}}\sqrt{|{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}|T\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}|}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\Big(\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}2^{-2{l}/3}\big({|{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1\to{l}}|\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}|}\big)^{1/3}\Big)^{3/2}\sqrt{T}\,.

The additional multiplicative factor of order at most L\sqrt{{{L}}} that we incur is due to the weaker feedback we are considering (two points vs L{{L}} observations per round). Crucially however, similar to what a more direct application of EXP4 would bring, this bound depends only on the logarithm of the total number of functions ln⁡|𝒢L|\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}|; that is, it does not feature the refined dependence we have on (ln⁡|𝒢l|)l≤L(\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{l}|)_{{l}\leq{{L}}}. As an effect, one would not be able to achieve T\sqrt{T} regret using such a bound in the examples considered in the next sections (where ln⁡|𝒢L|\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}| is polynomial in TT), which highlights the importance of relying on the policy tree and the nested regularizer.

3 A Concrete Rate

In this section, we provide a more explicit construction of the tree 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}), which will be designed to satisfy \Crefassump:function-tree while keeping 𝒢l{\mathcal{G}}_{l} and 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l} as small as possible. As such, the cardinalities of these sets will be expressed in terms of fundamental complexity (or size) properties of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}. Before proceeding, we recall some standard notions that we will be using next, all with respect to the metric 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and the metric 𝔡∞{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}} on policies from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

3.1 Complexity notions

For a∈𝒜a\in{\mathcal{A}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let B⁡(a,ε)≔{b∈𝒜∣𝔡⁡(a,b)≤ε}{B}(a;\varepsilon)\coloneqq\bigl\{b\in{\mathcal{A}}\mid{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b)\leq\varepsilon\bigr\} denote the ε\varepsilon-ball centered at aa.

Definition 3 (Covers and packings).

Let A⊆𝒜A\subseteq{\mathcal{A}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0.

  • •

    An ε\varepsilon-cover of AA is a set S⊆𝒜S\subseteq{\mathcal{A}} such that A⊆⋃a∈SB⁡(a,ε)A\subseteq\bigcup_{a\in S}{B}(a;\varepsilon), i.e., every point of AA is within distance ε\varepsilon of some point of SS. The covering number N⁡(A,ε){N}(A;\varepsilon) is the cardinality of the smallest ε\varepsilon-cover of AA.

  • •

    An ε\varepsilon-packing of AA is a subset of AA whose distinct members a≠ba\neq b all satisfy 𝔡⁡(a,b)>ε{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b)>\varepsilon. The packing number M⁡(A,ε){M}(A;\varepsilon) is the cardinality of the largest ε\varepsilon-packing of AA.

Covers and packings are equivalent up to a factor 22 in the scale: M⁡(A,2​ε)≤N⁡(A,ε)≤M⁡(A,ε).{M}(A;2\varepsilon)\leq{N}(A;\varepsilon)\leq{M}(A;\varepsilon)\,. The right inequality holds because a maximal ε\varepsilon-packing is automatically an ε\varepsilon-cover (a point of AA more than ε\varepsilon away from all its members could be added to it). The left one holds because a ball B⁡(a,ε){B}(a;\varepsilon) centered at a member of an ε\varepsilon-cover cannot contain two members of a 2​ε2\varepsilon-packing, as they would be at distance at most 2​ε2\varepsilon from each other. We use maximal packings to construct the action sets 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l}, since they are both covers and well-separated (which we will require), and covering numbers to measure complexity. For the policy classes, which are significantly larger, the relevant notion is the logarithm of the covering number in (𝒜𝒳,𝔡∞)({{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}},{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}), where 𝒜𝒳{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}} is the set of all functions from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

Definition 4 (Metric entropy).

For ℱ⊆𝒜𝒳{\mathcal{F}}\subseteq{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, let N⁡(ℱ,ε){N}({\mathcal{F}};\varepsilon) denote the covering number of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} in the metric space (𝒜𝒳,𝔡∞)({{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}},{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}). The metric entropy of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} at scale ε\varepsilon is H⁡(ℱ,ε)≔ln⁡N⁡(ℱ,ε){H}({\mathcal{F}};\varepsilon)\coloneqq\ln{N}({\mathcal{F}};\varepsilon).

3.2 Design of the hierarchical tree and concrete rates

With these notions in mind, we give now a general recipe for constructing the tree 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}). For the following, define C𝔡≔supa,b∈𝒜:a≠b𝔡(a,b){{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}\coloneqq\sup_{a,b\in{\mathcal{A}}\colon a\neq b}{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b), which is the diameter of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} w.r.t.\spacefactprè 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}}. Firstly, fix a sequence (𝒜l)l=0L({\mathcal{A}}_{l})_{{l}=0}^{{L}} of subsets of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} such that 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l} is a maximal C𝔡​2−l{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}-packing of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. This implies that 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l} is a C𝔡​2−l{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}-cover of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, and that |𝒜l|≤N⁡(𝒜,C𝔡​2−l−1)|{\mathcal{A}}_{l}|\leq{N}({\mathcal{A}};{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}-1}). Next, we will choose a sequence of sets of functions (ℱl)l=0L({\mathcal{F}}_{l})_{{l}=0}^{{L}} such that ℱl{\mathcal{F}}_{l} is a C𝔡​2−l+1{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}+1}-cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}, |ℱl|≤N⁡(𝒫,C𝔡​2−l)|{\mathcal{F}}_{l}|\leq{N}({\mathcal{P}};{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}), and img⁡(f)⊆𝒜l{\mathrm{img}}({f})\subseteq{\mathcal{A}}_{l} for all f∈ℱl{f}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{l}. In particular, these sets can be constructed as follows.

Let ℱ~l⊆𝒜𝒳\widetilde{{\mathcal{F}}}_{l}\subseteq{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}} be a C𝔡​2−l{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}-cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} satisfying |ℱ~l|=N(𝒫;C𝔡2−l)\bigl\lvert\widetilde{{\mathcal{F}}}_{l}\bigr\rvert={N}({\mathcal{P}};{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}). For any f∈𝒜𝒳{f}\in{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}}, let discl​(f)∈𝒜𝒳{\mathrm{disc}}_{l}({f})\in{{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathcal{X}}} be a discretization of f{f} onto 𝒜l{\mathcal{A}}_{l}; that is, discl​(f)​(x)∈arg​mina∈𝒜l⁡𝔡​(a,f⁡(x)){\mathrm{disc}}_{l}({f})(x)\in\argmin_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}_{l}}{\mathfrak{d}}(a,{f}(x)) for all x∈𝒳x\in{\mathcal{X}}. Hence, 𝔡∞​(f,discl​(f))≤C𝔡​2−l{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}\bigl({f},{\mathrm{disc}}_{l}({f})\bigr)\leq{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}. So, we can choose ℱl={discl​(f)∣f∈ℱ~l}{\mathcal{F}}_{l}=\bigl\{{\mathrm{disc}}_{l}({f})\mid{f}\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{F}}}_{l}\bigr\}, which is easily seen now (via the triangle inequality) to be a C𝔡​2−l+1{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}+1}-cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} as required. Note that since ℱ~l\widetilde{{\mathcal{F}}}_{l} is an optimal C𝔡​2−l{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}-cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}, it must be that for every f∈ℱ~l{f}\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{F}}}_{l}, there exists some 𝒽∈𝒫{\mathcal{h}}\in{\mathcal{P}} such that 𝔡∞​(𝒽,f)≤C𝔡​2−l{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({\mathcal{h}},{f})\leq{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}. The same then holds for ℱl{\mathcal{F}}_{l} at distance C𝔡​2−l+1{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}+1}.

We will use ℱl{\mathcal{F}}_{l} to populate 𝒢l{\mathcal{G}}_{l}, the nodes of the tree at level l{l}. To conclude the construction of the tree 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}), we need to specify the parenthood relation. Here, this can be any function such that for any f∈ℱl+1{f}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{{l}+1}, there exists some 𝒽∈𝒫{\mathcal{h}}\in{\mathcal{P}} satisfying 𝔡∞​(𝒽,f)≤C𝔡​2−l{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({\mathcal{h}},{f})\leq{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}} and 𝔡∞​(𝒽,𝔭⁡(f))≤C𝔡​2−l+1{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({\mathcal{h}},{\mathfrak{p}}({f}))\leq{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}+1}. This is possible since, as remarked before, each member of ℱl+1{\mathcal{F}}_{{l}+1} can be mapped to some 𝒽∈𝒫{\mathcal{h}}\in{\mathcal{P}} that is no more than C𝔡​2−l{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}} far, and ℱl{\mathcal{F}}_{l} is a C𝔡​2−l+1{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}+1}-cover of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}. As a consequence, for any f∈ℱl+1{f}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{{l}+1}, it holds via the triangle inequality that 𝔡∞​(f,𝔭⁡(f))≤3​C𝔡​2−l{\mathfrak{d}_{\infty}}({f},{\mathfrak{p}}({f}))\leq 3{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}2^{-{l}}. We see now that our new tree satisfies \Crefassump:function-tree with Capx=2​C𝔡{C}_{\mathrm{apx}}=2{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}} and Cprt=3​C𝔡{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}=3{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}. Then, building on \Crefthm:generic-thm, we establish the following guarantee for \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts. (The proof can be found in \Crefapp:concrete.)

Corollary 4.

Fix C𝒜,C𝒫>0{{C}}_{{\mathcal{A}}},{C}_{{\mathcal{P}}}>0 and take

d=inf{r≥0∣N⁡(𝒜,ε)≤C𝒜​(C𝔡/ε)r​∀ε∈(0,C𝔡]}\displaystyle{{d}}=\inf\bigl\{r\geq 0\mid{N}({\mathcal{A}};\varepsilon)\leq{{C}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}\bigl({{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}/\varepsilon\bigr)^{r}\>\forall\varepsilon\in(0,{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}]\bigr\}\qquad
and, p=inf{r≥0∣H⁡(𝒫,ε)≤C𝒫​(C𝔡/ε)r​∀ε∈(0,C𝔡]}.\displaystyle{{p}}=\inf\bigl\{r\geq 0\mid{H}({\mathcal{P}};\varepsilon)\leq{C}_{{\mathcal{P}}}\bigl({{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}/\varepsilon\bigr)^{r}\>\forall\varepsilon\in(0,{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}]\bigr\}\,.

Assume that log2⁡(T)≥(d+p)∨2\log_{2}(T)\geq({{d}}+{{p}})\lor 2. Then, tuned as in \Crefthm:generic-thm with Capx=2​C𝔡{C}_{\mathrm{apx}}=2{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}} and Cprt=3​C𝔡{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}=3{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}, \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts with 𝒯(𝒢0:L)\mathcal{T}({\mathcal{G}}_{0:{{L}}}) as described above and L=⌊log2⁡(T)/((d+p)∨2)⌋{{L}}=\bigl\lfloor{\log_{2}(T)}/{(({{d}}+{{p}})\lor 2)}\bigr\rfloor satisfies

RegT,2≤4​C𝔡​(24​C𝒜​C𝒫​ 4d∗+1)​ξ​(T,d,p)32​T1−1(d+p)∨2,\displaystyle\bm{\regret}_{T,2}\leq 4{{C}}_{{\mathfrak{d}}}\left(24\sqrt{{{C}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}{C}_{{\mathcal{P}}}}\,4^{{{{{d}}}^{*}}}+1\right){\xi}(T,{{d}},{{p}})^{\frac{3}{2}}\,T^{1-\frac{1}{({{d}}+{{p}})\lor 2}}\,,

where d∗≔inf{d≥0∣N(B(a;ε);ε/2)≤2d∀a∈𝒜,ε>0}{{{{d}}}^{*}}\coloneqq\inf\bigl\{d\geq 0\mid{N}\bigl({B}(a;\varepsilon);\varepsilon/2\bigr)\leq 2^{d}\>\forall a\in{\mathcal{A}},\varepsilon>0\bigr\} is the doubling dimension of (𝒜,𝔡)({\mathcal{A}},{\mathfrak{d}}), and ξ(T,d,p)≔|1−2−(d+p−2)/3|−1∧log2(T)/2.{\xi}(T,{{d}},{{p}})\coloneqq\bigl\lvert 1-2^{-({{d}}+{{p}}-2)/{3}}\bigr\rvert^{-1}\land{\log_{2}(T)}/{2}\,.

Essentially, the rate is T\sqrt{T} when d+p≤2{{d}}+{{p}}\leq 2 and T1−1/(d+p)T^{1-{1}/({{d}}+{{p}})} otherwise, up to a (log2⁡(T))3/2(\log_{2}(T))^{3/2} factor that appears when d+p{{d}}+{{p}} is around 22. Here, d{{d}} is the covering dimension of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} with multiplicity C𝒜{{C}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}, and p{{p}} is the metric entropy exponent of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} with multiplicity C𝒫{C}_{{\mathcal{P}}}. The derivation mostly follows from \Crefthm:generic-thm and the cardinality bounds we enforced in the construction. The crux is showing that 𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l​(a){\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}}(a) is bounded in terms of the doubling constant uniformly over l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}] and a∈𝒜a\in{\mathcal{A}}. This holds thanks to the proximity of a function and its parent, combined with the fact that, by construction, the image of a function at any level is a packing.

We now instantiate the bound of \Crefthm:concrete for some standard policy classes. We assume here that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a compact subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{{{{d}}}} and that 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} is the Euclidean distance. Using a uniform grid discretization, one can show that N⁡(𝒜,ε)≲ε−d{N}({\mathcal{A}};\varepsilon)\lesssim\varepsilon^{-{{{d}}}} up to a constant depending on d{{{d}}} and the diameter of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Moreover, the doubling dimension d∗{{{{d}}}^{*}} in this case is known to be 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}({{{d}}}) (Gupta et al., 2003). As for the contexts, we take 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} as a compact subset of ℝm\mathbb{R}^{{{m}}}.

Lipschitz Functions

Take the policy space to be the set of 11-Lipschitz functions mapping contexts to actions; so that ‖𝒽⁡(x)−𝒽⁡(x′)‖≤‖x−x′‖\|{\mathcal{h}}(x)-{\mathcal{h}}(x^{\prime})\|\leq\|x-x^{\prime}\| for 𝒽∈𝒫{\mathcal{h}}\in{\mathcal{P}} and x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{X}}. It can be shown that H⁡(𝒫,ε)≲ε−m{H}({\mathcal{P}};\varepsilon)\lesssim\varepsilon^{-{{{m}}}} with a constant depending on d{{{d}}}, m{{{m}}}, and the diameters of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}; an explicit construction is provided in \Crefsec:efficient. \Crefthm:concrete then implies that RegT,2\bm{\regret}_{T,2} is 𝒪⁡(ln⁡(T)3/2​T)\mathcal{O}(\ln(T)^{3/2}\sqrt{T}) when d=m=1{{{d}}}={{{m}}}=1 (essentially matching the full-information rate) and 𝒪⁡(T1−1/(d+m))\smash{\mathcal{O}(T^{1-{1}/({{{d}}}+{{{m}}})})} otherwise.

Hölder-Smooth Functions

Fix constants B,β,λ>0{B},{\beta},{\lambda}>0 and let β¯{\underline{{\beta}}} be the largest integer strictly smaller than β{\beta}. Take 𝒜=[−B,B]{\mathcal{A}}=[-{B},{B}] and 𝒳=[0,1]m{\mathcal{X}}=[0,1]^{{{m}}}. The policy set 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} now will consist of functions 𝒽:𝒳→ℝ{\mathcal{h}}\colon{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that for every 𝒌=(k1,…,km){\bm{k}}=({k}_{1},\dots,{k}_{{{m}}}) where ki{k}_{i} is an integer ≥0\geq 0 and 𝒌.≔∑i=1mki≤β¯{\bm{k}.}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{{{m}}}{k}_{i}\leq{\underline{{\beta}}}, supx∈𝒳|D𝒌​𝒽​(x)|≤B\sup_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}|D^{\bm{k}}{\mathcal{h}}(x)|\leq{B}, where D𝒌≔∂𝒌.∂x1k1​…​∂xmkm;D^{\bm{k}}\coloneqq\frac{\partial^{{\bm{k}.}}}{\partial x_{1}^{{k}_{1}}\dots\partial x_{{{m}}}^{{k}_{{{m}}}}}\,; moreover,

sup𝒌.=β¯supx,y∈𝒳|D𝒌​𝒽​(x)−D𝒌​𝒽​(y)|≤λ​‖x−y‖β−β¯.\sup_{{\bm{k}.}={\underline{{\beta}}}}\sup_{x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}|D^{\bm{k}}{\mathcal{h}}(x)-D^{\bm{k}}{\mathcal{h}}(y)|\leq{\lambda}\|x-y\|^{{\beta}-{\underline{{\beta}}}}\,.

Note that Lipschitz functions are recovered when β=1{\beta}=1. It holds here that H(𝒫;ε)≲ε−m/β{H}({\mathcal{P}};\varepsilon)\lesssim\varepsilon^{-{{{m}}}/{\beta}} with a constant depending on m{{{m}}}, β\beta, B{B}, and λ{\lambda}; see Theorem 2.7.1 in Van Der Vaart and Wellner (1996) or Theorem 2 in Lorentz (1962). So, we can take p=m/β{{p}}={{{m}}}/{\beta} and d=1{{d}}=1, in which case \Crefthm:concrete gives that RegT,2\bm{\regret}_{T,2} is 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) when β>m{\beta}>{{{m}}}, 𝒪⁡(ln⁡(T)3/2​T)\mathcal{O}(\ln(T)^{3/2}\sqrt{T}) when β=m{\beta}={{{m}}}, and 𝒪⁡(Tm/(m+β))\mathcal{O}\bigl(T^{{{{{m}}}}/({{{m}}}+{\beta})}\bigr) otherwise. In the first two cases, we match the full-information rate up to log factors.

4 An Efficient Implementation for Lipschitz Policies

In most interesting cases, the tree built in \Crefsec:concrete_rate is enormous and hence \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts would be intractable to implement. In this section, we focus on Lipschitz policy spaces and show that we can mimic the behaviour of \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts in an efficient manner when d{{{d}}} is small. This is possible by giving the function tree a structure that is separable in a certain sense, which allows us to devise more handy representations for objects acting on its constituent functions. For a clear presentation we will consider a simple setup with L∞L_{\infty} geometry. Concretely, we assume that 𝒳=[0,1]m{\mathcal{X}}=[0,1]^{{{m}}}, 𝒜=[0,1]d{\mathcal{A}}=[0,1]^{{{d}}}, and 𝔡⁡(a,b)=G​‖a−b‖∞{\mathfrak{d}}(a,b)={G}\|a-b\|_{\infty}. This implies that ℒ={ℓ:𝒜→ℝ∣|ℓ(a)−ℓ(b)|≤G∥a−b∥∞∀a,b∈𝒜}{\mathcal{L}}=\{{\ell}\colon{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\mid|{\ell}(a)-{\ell}(b)|\leq{G}\|a-b\|_{\infty}\>\forall a,b\in{\mathcal{A}}\}, i.e., the set of G{G}-Lipschitz functions from [0,1]d[0,1]^{{{d}}} to ℝ\mathbb{R} according to the L∞L_{\infty} metric. Lastly, assume that 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} is the set of 11-Lipschitz (in L∞L_{\infty}) functions mapping contexts to actions: 𝒫≔{𝒽:𝒳→𝒜∣∥𝒽(x)−𝒽(x′)∥∞≤∥x−x′∥∞∀x,x′∈𝒳}.{\mathcal{P}}\coloneqq\bigl\{{\mathcal{h}}\colon{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{A}}\mid\|{\mathcal{h}}(x)-{\mathcal{h}}(x^{\prime})\|_{\infty}\leq\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\>\forall\,x,x^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{X}}\bigr\}\,.

4.1 Building a structured tree

We start by building a nested partitioning (or a hierarchical discretization) of the context space. (Analogous approaches can be found, e.g., in Gaillard and Gerchinovitz, 2015.) For l≥0{l}\geq 0, define 𝒩l≔{(𝝂j)j≤l∣𝝂0=𝟏m​ and ​𝝂j∈{−1,1}m}{{\mathcal{N}}}_{l}\coloneqq\{({{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{j}})_{{{j}}\leq{l}}\mid{{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{0}=\mathbf{1}_{{{m}}}\text{ and }{{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{j}}\in\{-1,1\}^{{{m}}}\}, which satisfies |𝒩l|=2l​m|{{\mathcal{N}}}_{l}|=2^{{l}{{{m}}}}. A member of this set is essentially an address of a cell (subset) of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} in the partitioning associated with level l{l}. In particular, a sequence 𝝂=(𝝂j)j≤l∈𝒩l{{\bm{\nu}}}=({{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{j}})_{{{j}}\leq{l}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{l} can be used to identify a context ctx⁡(𝝂)≔∑j≤l2−j−1​𝝂j∈𝒳{{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\coloneqq\sum_{{{j}}\leq{l}}2^{-{{j}}-1}{{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{j}}\in{\mathcal{X}} and a cell which is the L∞L_{\infty} ball of radius 2−l−12^{-{l}-1} centered around ctx⁡(𝝂){{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}}).22 2 Precisely, to obtain non-overlapping boundaries, we define cell(𝝂)≔{x∈𝒳∣∀i∈[m],(⌊2lxi⌋+1)∧2l=⌊2lctx(𝝂)i⌋+1}{{\operatorname{cell}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\coloneqq\bigl\{x\in{\mathcal{X}}\mid\forall i\in[{{{m}}}]\,,\bigl(\lfloor 2^{{l}}x_{i}\rfloor+1\bigr)\land 2^{l}=\lfloor 2^{{l}}{{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})_{i}\rfloor+1\bigr\}. The cells {cell⁡(𝝂)}𝝂∈𝒩l\{{{\operatorname{cell}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\}_{{{\bm{\nu}}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{l}} form a uniform grid of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} with 2−l2^{-{l}} steps, and it holds that maxx∈cell⁡(𝝂)⁡‖x−ctx⁡(𝝂)‖∞≤2−l−1\max_{x\in{{\operatorname{cell}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})}\|x-{{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\|_{\infty}\leq 2^{-{l}-1}.

Fix 𝝂=(𝝂j)j≤l∈𝒩l{{\bm{\nu}}}=({{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{{j}}})_{{{j}}\leq{l}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{l}. The sub-sequence of 𝝂{{\bm{\nu}}} up to level l′{l}^{\prime} will be denoted by 𝝂:l′{{\bm{\nu}}}_{{{:}}{l}^{\prime}}, i.e., 𝝂:l′=(𝝂j)j≤l′{{\bm{\nu}}}_{{{:}}{l}^{\prime}}=({{{\bm{\nu}}}}_{{{j}}})_{{{j}}\leq{l}^{\prime}}. The set of children of 𝝂{{\bm{\nu}}} is given by 𝔠𝔥(𝝂)={𝝂′∈𝒩l+1∣𝝂:l′=𝝂}{\mathfrak{ch}}({{\bm{\nu}}})=\{{{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{l}+1}\mid{{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}_{{{:}}{l}}={{\bm{\nu}}}\}, and its parent is 𝔭(𝝂)=𝝂:l−1∈𝒩l−1{\mathfrak{p}}({{\bm{\nu}}})={{\bm{\nu}}}_{{{:}}{l}-1}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{l}-1}. It holds then that ‖ctx⁡(𝝂′)−ctx⁡(𝝂)‖∞≤2−l−2\|{{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime})-{{\operatorname{ctx}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\|_{\infty}\leq 2^{-{l}-2} for all 𝝂′∈𝔠​𝔥​(𝝂){{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}\in{\mathfrak{ch}}({{\bm{\nu}}}). A crucial property is that cell⁡(𝝂)⊂cell⁡(𝔭⁡(𝝂)){{\operatorname{cell}}}({{\bm{\nu}}})\subset{{\operatorname{cell}}}({\mathfrak{p}}({{\bm{\nu}}})); meaning that the partitions are nested across levels. For x∈𝒳x\in{\mathcal{X}}, let seq⁡(x)=(seqj⁡(x))j≤L{{\operatorname{seq}}}(x)=({{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{j}}(x))_{{{j}}\leq{{L}}} denote the unique node in 𝒩L{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{L}} to whose cell xx belongs, and let seq:l(x)=(seqj(x))j≤l{{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}}(x)=({{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{j}}(x))_{{{j}}\leq{l}} be its ancestor at level l{l}.

For convenience, we will give ourselves the freedom of selecting actions within the extended set 𝒜+=[−1,2]d{\mathcal{A}}^{+}=[-1,2]^{{{d}}} with the understanding that ℓ⁡(a)=ℓ⁡(clip⁡(a)){\ell}(a)={\ell}(\clip(a)), where clip⁡(a)i=1∧(0∨ai)\clip(a)_{i}=1\land(0\lor a_{i}). These extended loss functions are still G{G}-Lipschitz since

|ℓ⁡(a)−ℓ⁡(b)|=|ℓ⁡(clip⁡(a))−ℓ⁡(clip⁡(b))|≤G​‖clip⁡(a)−clip⁡(b)‖∞≤G​‖a−b‖∞.|{\ell}(a)-{\ell}(b)|=|{\ell}(\clip(a))-{\ell}(\clip(b))|\leq{G}\|\clip(a)-\clip(b)\|_{\infty}\leq{G}\|a-b\|_{\infty}\,.

On the computational complexity

We now argue that \Crefalg:efficient is efficient: it has a space complexity of 𝒪⁡(T​ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\ln T) and a per-round time complexity of 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T). Here we assume that d{{{d}}} is small and treat it as constant. Observe that L≲ln⁡T{{L}}\lesssim\ln T, |𝒩L|≲Tm/(d+m)|{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{L}}|\lesssim T^{{{{m}}}/({{{d}}}+{{{m}}})}, |𝒜L|≲Td/(d+m)|{\mathcal{A}}_{{{L}}}|\lesssim T^{{{{d}}}/({{{d}}}+{{{m}}})}, and the size of the successor set of any action is 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). Hence, storing the functions ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} and ϕt,𝝂{\bm{\phi}}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} for all 𝝂∈𝒩0:L{{\bm{\nu}}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{0:{{L}}} has a complexity of at most 𝒪⁡(T​ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\ln T). Having stored these functions, sampling the two paths (at,l)l≤L({a}_{t,{l}})_{{l}\leq{{L}}} and (at,l′)l≤L({a}^{\prime}_{t,{l}})_{{l}\leq{{L}}} requires 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T) computations since the support of πt,𝝂(⋅∣a){\pi}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}(\cdot\mid a) is the successor set of aa. Another burdensome step is updating the functions ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}. For l∈{0,…,L−1}{l}\in\{0,\dots,{{L}}-1\}, 𝝂∈𝒩l{{\bm{\nu}}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{l}}, and a∈𝒜la\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}}, ωt,𝝂​(a){\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}(a) is defined as (see \Creflem:efficient:exp-profiles-closed-form in \Crefapp:efficient:dec)

ωt,𝝂(a)≔∑𝝂′∈𝔠​𝔥​(𝝂)−Λl+1ln(∑b∈𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l+1​(a)exp(−Λl+1−1(ϕt,𝝂′(b,a)+ωt,𝝂′(b)))),\displaystyle{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}(a)\coloneqq\sum_{{{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}\in{\mathfrak{ch}}({{\bm{\nu}}})}-{\Lambda}_{{l}+1}\ln\left(\sum_{b\in{\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}+1}(a)}\exp\Bigl(-{\Lambda}^{-1}_{{l}+1}\bigl({\bm{\phi}}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}}(b,a)+{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}^{\prime}}(b)\bigr)\Bigr)\right)\,, (2)

while for 𝝂∈𝒩L{{\bm{\nu}}}\in{{\mathcal{N}}}_{{{L}}} and a∈𝒜La\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{{L}}}, set ωt,𝝂​(a)≔0{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}(a)\coloneqq 0. We discuss next the complexity of these updates.

Recall that we denote by seq⁡(xt){{\operatorname{seq}}}(x_{t}) the sequence of context nodes (at each level of the tree) to which xtx_{t} belongs. Now ϕt,𝝂{\bm{\phi}}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} will only be updated (i.e., incremented compared to its value at the previous round) for 𝝂{{\bm{\nu}}} lying in said path, and hence the same holds for ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}}. In fact, only ϕt,𝓿t​(Bt,1,Bt,2)\displaystyle{\bm{\phi}}_{t,{{\bm{\mathcal{v}}}}_{t}}({B}_{t,1},{B}_{t,2}) is updated at round tt, where 𝓿t=seq:lt(xt){{\bm{\mathcal{v}}}}_{t}={{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}_{t}}(x_{t}). This implies via (2) that ϕt,𝝂{\bm{\phi}}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} and ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} will remain unchanged for all nodes in (seq:l(xt))l≥lt({{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}}(x_{t}))_{{l}\geq{l}_{t}}. It is ωt,𝔭⁡(𝓿t)\omega_{t,{\mathfrak{p}}({{\bm{\mathcal{v}}}}_{t})} that is first updated, and only at the action Bt,2{B}_{t,2}. This change must then be propagated upwards to ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} for all nodes 𝝂{{\bm{\nu}}} in (seq:l(xt))l≤lt−2({{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}}(x_{t}))_{{l}\leq{l}_{t}-2}. Inspecting (2) again, we can see that at any of these nodes, say node 𝝂{{\bm{\nu}}} at level l{l}, ωt,𝝂{\omega}_{t,{{\bm{\nu}}}} needs to be updated only at actions a∈𝒜la\in{\mathcal{A}}_{l} from which it is possible to construct a downwards path (a,…,Bt,2)(a,\dots,{B}_{t,2}) to lt−1{l}_{t}-1 with each action belonging to the successor set of the previous. In \Crefapp:efficient:pre, we call this set of actions Phys.Rev.El​(Bt,2){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}({B}_{t,2}) and show that, luckily, |Phys.Rev.El(Bt,2)|≤3d|{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}({B}_{t,2})|\leq 3^{{{d}}} uniformly at all levels. This implies that we only need to carry out 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T) updates.

Finally, given l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}], a∈𝒜l−1a\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1}, and b∈𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l​(a)b\in{\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}}(a); we need to be able to compute ℙt​(Bt,1=b,Bt,2=a∣lt=l)\mathbb{P}_{t}({B}_{t,1}=b,{B}_{t,2}=a\mid{l}_{t}={l}). Since Bt,1=at,lt{B}_{t,1}={a}_{t,{l}_{t}}, Bt,2=at,lt−1{B}_{t,2}={a}_{t,{l}_{t}-1}, and lt{l}_{t} is independent of (at,l)l≤L({a}_{t,{l}})_{{l}\leq{{L}}}; it holds that ℙt(Bt,1=b,Bt,2=a∣lt=l)=ℙt(at,l=b,at,l−1=a)=ℙt(at,l−1=a)πt,seq:l(xt)(b∣a)\mathbb{P}_{t}({B}_{t,1}=b,{B}_{t,2}=a\mid{l}_{t}={l})=\mathbb{P}_{t}({a}_{t,{l}}=b,{a}_{t,{l}-1}=a)=\mathbb{P}_{t}({a}_{t,{l}-1}=a){\pi}_{t,{{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}}(x_{t})}(b\mid a). On the other hand, ℙt(at,l−1=a)=∑a′∈Phys.Rev.El−2​(a)ℙt(at,l−2=a′)πt,seq:l−1(xt)(a∣a′)\mathbb{P}_{t}({a}_{t,{l}-1}=a)=\sum_{a^{\prime}\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}-2}(a)}\mathbb{P}_{t}({a}_{t,{l}-2}=a^{\prime}){\pi}_{t,{{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}-1}(x_{t})}(a\mid a^{\prime}). Iterating this upwards, we see that, in addition to πt,seq:l(xt)(b∣a){\pi}_{t,{{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{l}}(x_{t})}(b\mid a), we need to compute the conditional probabilities πt,seq:j(xt)(c∣c′){\pi}_{t,{{\operatorname{seq}}}_{{{:}}{{j}}}(x_{t})}(c\mid c^{\prime}) for all pairs c∈Phys.Rev.Ej​(a),c′∈Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(a)c\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}}(a),c^{\prime}\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(a) for j=l−1,…,1{{j}}={l}-1,\dots,1. Since, again, Phys.Rev.Ej​(⋅){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}}(\cdot) is uniformly bounded independently of j{{j}}, we conclude that the complexity of this procedure is still 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T). All in all, we see that the per-round complexity of \Crefalg:efficient is 𝒪⁡(ln⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\ln T).

Some elements of the efficient algorithm of \Crefsec:efficient were arrived at thanks to interactions with Claude (various models). Otherwise, AI use was limited to proofreading and proof verification.

where the first inequality uses the second part of \Crefassump:function-tree seeing as 𝔞​𝔫l−1​(⋅)=𝔭⁡(𝔞​𝔫l​(⋅)){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}(\cdot)}={\mathfrak{p}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}(\cdot)}). In a similar fashion, we can write

𝔡⁡(At,2,𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt))\displaystyle{\mathfrak{d}}\bigl(A_{t,2},{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})\bigr) =𝔡⁡(ft,2​(xt),𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(ft,2)​(xt))\displaystyle={\mathfrak{d}}\bigl({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}),{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})\bigr)
=∑l=ltL𝔡⁡(𝔞​𝔫l​(ft,2)​(xt),𝔞​𝔫l−1​(ft,2)​(xt))\displaystyle=\sum_{{l}={l}_{t}}^{{{L}}}{\mathfrak{d}}\bigl({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t}),{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})\bigr)
≤∑l=ltLCprt​2−l+1≤Cprt​2−lt+2.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{{l}={l}_{t}}^{{{L}}}{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}+1}\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}_{t}+2}\,.

Then, we can conclude by using the triangle inequality one more time, combined with the definition of 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}}:

|ℓt​(At,1)−ℓt​(At,2)|\displaystyle|{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})| ≤𝔡⁡(At,1,At,2)\displaystyle\leq{\mathfrak{d}}(A_{t,1},A_{t,2})
≤𝔡⁡(At,1,𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt))+𝔡⁡(At,2,𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt))\displaystyle\leq{\mathfrak{d}}\bigl(A_{t,1},{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})\bigr)+{\mathfrak{d}}\bigl(A_{t,2},{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})\bigr)
≤Cprt​2−lt+3.\displaystyle\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}_{t}+3}\,.

∎

Lemma 8.

Choosing bl=Cprt​2−l+3b_{l}={C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}+3} at every level guarantees that

0≤ℓt​(At,1)−ℓt​(At,2)+blt≤Cprt​2−lt+4.0\leq{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}_{t}+4}\,.
Proof.

Since \Creflem:loss-diff-bound gives that |ℓt​(At,1)−ℓt​(At,2)|≤Cprt​2−lt+3|{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})|\leq{C}_{\mathrm{prt}}2^{-{l}_{t}+3}, the stated choice of blb_{l} yields the lemma’s statement. ∎

Lemma 9.

For l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}] and f∈𝒢l{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l}, define

𝐜^t,l​(f)≔⟦Bt,1=f(xt),Bt,2=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)ℙt​[Bt,1=f⁡(xt),Bt,2=𝔭⁡(f)​(xt),lt=l].{\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}({f})\coloneqq\frac{\llbracket{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={\mathfrak{p}}({f})(x_{t})\,,\,{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\mathbb{P}_{t}[{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={\mathfrak{p}}({f})(x_{t})\,,\,{l}_{t}={l}]}\,.

Then, for any f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{{L}}},

𝐜^t​(f)=∑l=1L𝐜^t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f)).\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f})=\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}{\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})})\,.
Proof.

For f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} and l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}], define

Et​(f,l)≔{Bt,1=𝔞​𝔫l​(f)​(xt),Bt,2=𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)​(xt)}.{E}_{t}({f},{l})\coloneqq\{{B}_{t,1}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t})\}\,.

Observe then that 𝐜^t​(f)\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f}), as defined in \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts, can be written as

𝐜^t​(f)\displaystyle\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f}) =⟦Et​(f,lt)⟧​(ℓt​(At,1)−ℓt​(At,2)+blt)δlt​ℙt​[Et​(f,lt)∣lt]\displaystyle=\frac{\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}_{t})\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\delta_{{l}_{t}}\mathbb{P}_{t}[{E}_{t}({f},{l}_{t})\mid{l}_{t}]}
=∑l=1L⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)δl​ℙt​[Et​(f,l)∣lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt=\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}\frac{\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\delta_{{l}}\mathbb{P}_{t}[{E}_{t}({f},{l})\mid{l}_{t}={l}]}
=∑l=1L⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)ℙt[lt=l]ℙt[Et(f,l)∣lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt=\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}\frac{\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\mathbb{P}_{t}[{l}_{t}={l}]\mathbb{P}_{t}[{E}_{t}({f},{l})\mid{l}_{t}={l}]}
=∑l=1L⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)ℙt​[Et​(f,l),lt=l],\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt=\sum_{{l}=1}^{{{L}}}\frac{\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\mathbb{P}_{t}[{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}]}\,,

where we have used that δl=ℙt​(lt=l)\delta_{l}=\mathbb{P}_{t}({l}_{t}={l}). The lemma then follows from the definition of 𝐜^t,l​(⋅){\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}(\cdot) and the fact that 𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)=𝔭⁡(𝔞​𝔫l​(f)){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}={\mathfrak{p}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}). ∎

Lemma 10.

For l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}] and f∈𝒢l{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l}, it holds that

𝔼t[𝐜^t,l(f)]=𝔼t[ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt∣Bt,1=f(xt),Bt,2=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l].\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}({f})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\mid{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t})\,,\,{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]\,.
Proof.

Observe from the proof of \Creflem:estnodeloss that we can write

𝐜^t,l​(f)=⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)ℙt​[Et​(f,l),lt=l],\displaystyle{\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}({f})=\frac{\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)}{\mathbb{P}_{t}[{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}]}\,,

where

Et​(f,l)={Bt,1=𝔞​𝔫l​(f)​(xt),Bt,2=𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)​(xt)}={Bt,1=f⁡(xt),Bt,2=𝔭⁡(f)​(xt)}.{E}_{t}({f},{l})=\{{B}_{t,1}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t})\}=\{{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t})\}\,.

The second equality above holds since f{f} here is a member of 𝒢l{\mathcal{G}}_{l}. Taking the expectation of the numerator yields

𝔼t[⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)\right]
=ℙt[Et(f,l),lt=l]𝔼t[⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)∣Et(f,l),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt=\mathbb{P}_{t}\bigl[{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)\mid{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\right]
+ℙt[Et​(f,l)¯∨lt≠l]𝔼t[⟦Et(f,l),lt=l⟧(ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt)∣Et​(f,l)¯∨lt≠l]\displaystyle\hskip 25.00003pt+\mathbb{P}_{t}\Bigl[\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu{E}_{t}({f},{l})\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu\lor{l}_{t}\neq{l}\Bigr]\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\llbracket{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\rrbracket\bigl({\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\bigr)\mid\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu{E}_{t}({f},{l})\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu\lor{l}_{t}\neq{l}\right]
=ℙt[Et(f,l),lt=l]𝔼t[ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt∣Et(f,l),lt=l].\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt=\mathbb{P}_{t}\bigl[{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\mid{E}_{t}({f},{l}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]\,.

The lemma then follows since the denominator of 𝐜^t,l​(f){\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}}_{t,{l}}({f}) is 𝔉t−1{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t-1}-measurable. ∎

Recall that we have defined 𝐜t​(f)≔ℓt​(f⁡(xt)){\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})\coloneqq{\ell}_{t}({f}(x_{t})) for f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}.

Lemma 11.

For l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}] and f∈𝒢l{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l}, define

𝐜t,l(f)≔𝔼t[ℓt(At,1)−ℓt(At,2)+blt∣Bt,1=f(xt),Bt,2=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l].\displaystyle{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({f})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})-{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})+b_{{l}_{t}}\mid{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t})\,,\,{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t})\,,\,{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]\,.

Then, any f,f′∈𝒢L{f},{f}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} satisfy that

𝐜t​(f)−𝐜t​(f′)=∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f))−∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f′)).\displaystyle{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})-{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f}^{\prime})=\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})})-\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}^{\prime})})\,.
Proof.

Observe that

𝔼t[ℓt(At,1)∣Bt,1=f(xt),Bt,2=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})\mid{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t}),{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,1(xt))∣𝔞𝔫lt(gt)(xt)=f(xt),𝔞𝔫lt−1(gt)(xt)=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={f}(x_{t}),{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,1(xt))∣𝔞𝔫lt(gt)(xt)=f(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={f}(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,1(xt))∣𝔞𝔫l(ft,1)(xt)=f(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t})={f}(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,1​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫l​(ft,1)​(xt)=f⁡(xt)],\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t})={f}(x_{t})\bigr]\,,

where the first step uses the definitions of At,1A_{t,1}, Bt,1{B}_{t,1}, and Bt,2{B}_{t,2}; the second uses the fact that knowing lt{l}_{t} and 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t}), ft,1{f}_{t,1} is independent of 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}; the third uses that 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫lt​(ft,1)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t}); and the last equality uses that ft,1⟂⁣⟂lt|𝔉t−1{f}_{t,1}\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\!\perp}{l}_{t}\mid{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t-1} as asserts \Creflem:same-marginals-independent-from-level. In a similar manner,

𝔼t[ℓt(At,2)∣Bt,1=f(xt),Bt,2=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})\mid{B}_{t,1}={f}(x_{t}),{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,2(xt))∣𝔞𝔫lt(gt)(xt)=f(xt),𝔞𝔫lt−1(gt)(xt)=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={f}(x_{t}),{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,2(xt))∣𝔞𝔫lt−1(gt)(xt)=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t[ℓt(ft,2(xt))∣𝔞𝔫l−1(ft,2)(xt)=𝔭(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
=𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,2​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫l−1​(ft,2)​(xt)=𝔭⁡(f)​(xt)],\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{p}}}({f})(x_{t})\bigr]\,,

where the first step uses the definitions of At,2A_{t,2}, Bt,1{B}_{t,1}, and Bt,2{B}_{t,2}; the second uses the fact that knowing lt{l}_{t} and 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t}), ft,2{f}_{t,2} is independent of 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}; the third uses that 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(ft,2)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t}); and the last equality uses that ft,2⟂⁣⟂lt|𝔉t−1{f}_{t,2}\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\!\perp}{l}_{t}\mid{{\mathfrak{F}}}_{t-1} via \Creflem:same-marginals-independent-from-level. Hence, it holds for any f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} that

∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f))\displaystyle\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}) =∑l∈[L]𝔼t[ℓt(At,1)∣Bt,1=𝔞𝔫l(f)(xt),Bt,2=𝔞𝔫l−1(f)(xt),lt=l]\displaystyle=\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,1})\mid{B}_{t,1}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t}),{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]
−𝔼t[ℓt(At,2)∣Bt,1=𝔞𝔫l(f)(xt),Bt,2=𝔞𝔫l−1(f)(xt),lt=l]+bl\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt-\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})\mid{B}_{t,1}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t}),{B}_{t,2}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t}),{l}_{t}={l}\bigr]+b_{{l}}
=∑l∈[L]𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,1​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫l​(ft,1)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫l​(f)​(xt)]\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt=\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})}(x_{t})\bigr]
−𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,2​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫l−1​(ft,2)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f)​(xt)]+bl\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt-\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}(x_{t})\bigr]+b_{{l}}
=𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,1​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫L​(ft,1)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫L​(f)​(xt)]\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,1}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{{L}}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{{L}}}({f})}(x_{t})\bigr]
−𝔼t​[ℓt​(ft,2​(xt))∣𝔞​𝔫0​(ft,2)​(xt)=𝔞​𝔫0​(f)​(xt)]+∑l∈[L]bl\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt-\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}({f}_{t,2}(x_{t}))\mid{{\mathfrak{an}}_{0}({f}_{t,2})}(x_{t})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{0}({f})}(x_{t})\bigr]+\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}b_{{l}}
=ℓt​(f⁡(xt))−𝔼t​[ℓt​(At,2)]+∑l∈[L]bl=𝐜t​(f)−𝔼t​[ℓt​(At,2)]+∑l∈[L]bl,\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt={\ell}_{t}({f}(x_{t}))-\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})\bigr]+\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}b_{{l}}={\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})-\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[{\ell}_{t}(A_{t,2})\bigr]+\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}b_{{l}}\,,

where the first equality holds since 𝔭⁡(𝔞​𝔫l​(f))=𝔞​𝔫l−1​(f){{\mathfrak{p}}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})})={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}-1}({f})}; the second uses the previous two derivations; the third uses the telescoping property of the sum, which follows since ℙt​(ft,1)=ℙt​(ft,2)\mathbb{P}_{t}({f}_{t,1})=\mathbb{P}_{t}({f}_{t,2}) via \Creflem:same-marginals-independent-from-level; and the fourth uses that 𝔞​𝔫L​(f)=f{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{{L}}}({f})}={f} and 𝔞​𝔫0​(f)=f0{{\mathfrak{an}}_{0}({f})}={f}_{0} for all f∈𝒢L{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}. As a consequence, any f,f′∈𝒢L{f},{f}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} satisfy, as required, that

∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f))−∑l∈[L]𝐜t,l​(𝔞​𝔫l​(f′))=𝐜t​(f)−𝐜t​(f′).\displaystyle\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f})})-\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t,{l}}({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}^{\prime})})={\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})-{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f}^{\prime})\,.

∎

Lemma 12.

For any f,f′∈𝒢L{f},{f}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}, it holds that

𝐜t​(f)−𝐜t​(f′)=𝔼t​[𝐜^t​(f)−𝐜^t​(f′)].\displaystyle{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})-{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f})-\widehat{{\mathbf{c}}}_{t}({f}^{\prime})\bigr]\,.
Proof.

Combining \Creflem:estnodeloss,lem:expectation-of-estnodeloss,lem:telescoping-nodeloss, we get

=𝐜t​(f)−𝐜t​(f′).\displaystyle={\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f})-{\mathbf{c}}_{t}({f}^{\prime})\,.

∎

Auxiliary results

The following Lemma is a direct adaptation of Lemma 16 in Eldowa et al. (2026) to the nested negative entropy regularizer.

Lemma 14.

Let (ηt,l)t≥1,l∈[L](\eta_{t,{l}})_{t\geq 1,{l}\in[{{L}}]} be a sequence of positive numbers. For every t≥1t\geq 1, let ψt\psi_{t} be given by ψt​(p)=∑l∈[L]1ηt,l​∑f∈𝒢lp⁡[f]​ln⁡p⁡[f]\psi_{t}(p)=\sum_{{l}\in[{{L}}]}\frac{1}{\eta_{t,{l}}}\sum_{{f}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l}}p[{f}]\ln p[{f}] for p∈Δ𝒢,Lp\in{{\Delta}}_{{\mathcal{G}},{{L}}}. Let (𝐳t)t({\bm{z}}_{t})_{t} be a sequence of loss functions mapping 𝒢L{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}} to ℝ\mathbb{R}, and define

C.2 Decomposing the sampling distribution

For completeness, the following lemma provides a standard result regarding the minimization, over the simplex, of a linear function minus the entropy function H⁡(p)≔∑i=1dp⁡(i)​ln⁡(1/p⁡(i))H(p)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d}p(i)\ln(1/p(i)).

Lemma 19.

Fix any y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and define p∗=arg​minp∈Δd⁡⟨p,y⟩−H⁡(p).\displaystyle p^{*}=\argmin_{p\in\Delta_{d}}\langle p,y\rangle-H(p)\,. Then,

p[𝜽]≔∑𝜽′∈𝒢L⟦𝜽=𝔞𝔫l(𝜽′)⟧p(𝜽′).\displaystyle p[{{\bm{\theta}}}]\coloneqq\sum_{{{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}}\llbracket{{\bm{\theta}}}={{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime})}\rrbracket p({{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime})\,.

When this pertains to ptp_{t} at some round tt, we use the notation pt,lp_{t,{l}}. For l∈{0,…,L−1}{l}\in\{0,\dots,{{L}}-1\}, 𝜽∈𝒢l{{\bm{\theta}}}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{l}, and p∈Δ𝒢,Lp\in{{\Delta}}_{{\mathcal{G}},{{L}}} such that p⁡[𝜽]>0p[{{\bm{\theta}}}]>0, let π𝜽p{\pi}_{{{\bm{\theta}}}}^{p} be a conditional distribution over 𝔠​𝔥​(𝜽){\mathfrak{ch}}({{\bm{\theta}}}) given by

π𝜽p​(𝜽′)=p⁡[𝜽′]p⁡[𝜽]∀𝜽′∈𝔠​𝔥​(𝜽).{\pi}_{{{\bm{\theta}}}}^{p}({{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime})=\frac{p[{{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime}]}{p[{{\bm{\theta}}}]}\quad\forall{{\bm{\theta}}}^{\prime}\in{\mathfrak{ch}}({{\bm{\theta}}})\,.

Thus, for any 𝜽∈𝒢L{{\bm{\theta}}}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{{L}}} with p⁡(𝜽)>0p({{\bm{\theta}}})>0, we can, since p⁡[𝜽0]=1p[{{\bm{\theta}}}_{0}]=1, write

p⁡(𝜽)=∏l∈{0,…,L−1}π𝔞​𝔫l​(𝜽)p​(𝔞​𝔫l+1​(𝜽)).p({{\bm{\theta}}})=\prod_{{l}\in\{0,\dots,{{L}}-1\}}{\pi}_{{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({{\bm{\theta}}})}^{p}({\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}+1}({{\bm{\theta}}}))\,.
Lemma 20.

Fix any Y:𝒢L→ℝ{{Y}}\colon{\mathcal{G}}_{{L}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and let q=arg​minp∈Δ𝒢,L⁡⟨p,Y⟩+ψ⁡(p)\displaystyle q=\argmin_{p\in{{\Delta}}_{{\mathcal{G}},{{L}}}}\left\langle p,{{Y}}\right\rangle+\psi(p), where

The following is a proof of \Crefthm:efficient, which we restate below. See 5

Proof.

As noted in \Crefsec:efficient:alg, \Crefalg:efficient mimics the sampling process of \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts. To be precise, the path (at,l)l≤L({a}_{t,{l}})_{{l}\leq{{L}}} plays the role of (𝔞​𝔫l​(gt)​(xt))l≤L({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t}))_{{l}\leq{{L}}}, which gives indeed that Bt,1=at,lt{B}_{t,1}={a}_{t,{l}_{t}} and Bt,2=at,lt−1.{B}_{t,2}={a}_{t,{l}_{t}-1}. Finally, we do not sample a third path like \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts; instead, we use (at,l)l≤L({a}_{t,{l}})_{{l}\leq{{L}}} to also play the role of (𝔞​𝔫l​(ft,1)​(xt))l≤L({{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}}({f}_{t,1})}(x_{t}))_{{l}\leq{{L}}} and set At,1=at,LA_{t,1}={a}_{t,{{L}}}. Taking ft,1=gt{f}_{t,1}={g}_{t} does not pose a problem in the analysis of \Crefalg:2-point-feedback-experts as long as gt​(xt){g}_{t}(x_{t}) is independent of 𝔞​𝔫lt−1​(gt)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}-1}({g}_{t})}(x_{t}) given lt{l}_{t} and 𝔞​𝔫lt​(gt)​(xt){{\mathfrak{an}}_{{l}_{t}}({g}_{t})}(x_{t}). This holds true here thanks to the factorized form of ptp_{t}.

At every l{l}, it holds that |𝒜l|≤3d​2l​d|{\mathcal{A}}_{l}|\leq 3^{{{d}}}2^{{l}{{{d}}}}, maxa∈𝒜l−1⁡|𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l​(a)|=4d\max_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}-1}}|{\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}}(a)|=4^{{{d}}}, and ln⁡|𝒢l|≤ln⁡(4)​d​2m​2l​m\ln|{\mathcal{G}}_{l}|\leq\ln(4){{{d}}}2^{{{m}}}2^{{l}{{{m}}}}. C.4 The predecessor set

For every l∈{0,…,L}{l}\in\{0,\dots,{{L}}\}, we define a function Phys.Rev.El:𝒜j≥l→2𝒜l{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}\colon{\mathcal{A}}_{{{j}}\geq{l}}\rightarrow 2^{{\mathcal{A}}_{l}} given by Phys.Rev.El​(b)≔{b}{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}(b)\coloneqq\{b\} for b∈𝒜lb\in{\mathcal{A}}_{l}, by Phys.Rev.El​(b)≔{a∈𝒜l∣b∈𝔰​𝔲​𝔠l+1​(a)}{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}(b)\coloneqq\{a\in{\mathcal{A}}_{l}\mid b\in{\mathfrak{suc}}_{{l}+1}(a)\} for b∈𝒜l+1b\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{l}+1}, and by Phys.Rev.El​(b)≔⋃a∈Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(b)Phys.Rev.El​(a){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}(b)\coloneqq\bigcup_{a\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b)}{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}(a) for b∈𝒜jb\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{j}} with j≥l+2{{j}}\geq{l}+2. From one level to the previous, this function is the reverse of the successor relation. Going further up, we end up with the set of all actions that can lead to the action in question via a sequence of actions respecting the successor relation. The following result provides a uniform upper bound for Phys.Rev.El​(⋅){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{l}}(\cdot).

Lemma 22.

In the tree of \Crefsec:efficient:tree, it holds for any l∈[L]{l}\in[{{L}}] and b∈𝒜j≥lb\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{{j}}\geq{l}} that |Phys.Rev.El(b)|≤3d|{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{l}(b)|\leq 3^{{{{d}}}}.

Proof.

Fix some j>l{{j}}>{l} and b∈𝒜jb\in{\mathcal{A}}_{{j}}. Any a∈Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(b)a\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b) satisfies that ‖a−b‖∞≤3⋅2−j−1\|a-b\|_{\infty}\leq 3\cdot 2^{-{{j}}-1}. Therefore, Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(b){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b) is contained in an L∞L_{\infty} ball of radius 3⋅2−j−13\cdot 2^{-{{j}}-1} (or diameter 3⋅2−j=(3/2)⋅2−j+13\cdot 2^{-{{j}}}=(3/2)\cdot 2^{-{{j}}+1}) centered at bb. At the same time, Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(b){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b) is a subset of 𝒜j−1{\mathcal{A}}_{{{j}}-1} which is a 2−j+12^{-{{j}}+1} spaced grid. Hence, |Phys.Rev.Ej−1(b)|≤2d|{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b)|\leq 2^{{{d}}}. Moving upwards, Phys.Rev.Ej−2​(a){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-2}(a) is contained in an L∞L_{\infty} ball of radius 3⋅2−j3\cdot 2^{-{{j}}} centered at aa for all a∈Phys.Rev.Ej−1​(b)a\in{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-1}(b). Hence, Phys.Rev.Ej−2​(b){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-2}(b) is contained in an L∞L_{\infty} ball of diameter 9⋅2−j=(9/4)⋅2−j+29\cdot 2^{-{{j}}}=({9}/{4})\cdot 2^{-{{j}}+2}. This is now a subset of 𝒜j−2{\mathcal{A}}_{{{j}}-2}, which is a 2−j+22^{-{{j}}+2} spaced grid, implying that |Phys.Rev.Ej−2(b)|≤3d|{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{{{j}}-2}(b)|\leq 3^{{{d}}}. Iterating this argument, we obtain a series (yk)k=j−1,…,l(y_{k})_{k={{j}}-1,\dots,{l}} with yj−1=3/2y_{{{j}}-1}=3/2 and yk=(yk+1+3)/2y_{k}=(y_{k+1}+3)/2, such that Phys.Rev.Ek​(b){\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{k}(b) is contained in an L∞L_{\infty} ball of diameter yk⋅2−ky_{k}\cdot 2^{-k}. Since for any kk, yk<3y_{k}<3 and 𝒜k{\mathcal{A}}_{k} is a 2−k2^{-k} spaced grid, we obtain that |Phys.Rev.Ek(b)|≤3d|{\rm Phys.~Rev.~E}_{k}(b)|\leq 3^{{{d}}}. ∎
